passages.title: The Respiratory System
passages.text: The respiratory system is the group of organs responsible for taking in oxygen and removing carbon dioxide from the body. It includes the nose, nasal cavity, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles and lungs. Breathing supplies oxygen for cellular respiration and removes the waste gas carbon dioxide.

passages.title: Breathing and Respiration
passages.text: Breathing, or ventilation, is the physical movement of air into and out of the lungs. Cellular respiration is the chemical process inside cells that releases energy from glucose using oxygen and producing carbon dioxide and water. Breathing supplies the oxygen needed for respiration and removes the carbon dioxide it produces.

passages.title: Nose and Nasal Cavity
passages.text: Air enters through the nose and nasal cavity, where it is warmed, moistened and filtered. Tiny hairs and mucus trap dust and microbes, cleaning the air before it reaches the lungs. This protects the delicate lung tissue from damage and infection.

passages.title: The Trachea
passages.text: The trachea, or windpipe, is a tube that carries air from the larynx down towards the lungs. It is supported by C-shaped rings of cartilage that keep it open. The trachea is lined with cilia and mucus that trap and sweep dust and pathogens upward away from the lungs.

passages.title: Bronchi and Bronchioles
passages.text: The trachea divides into two bronchi, one entering each lung. Each bronchus branches repeatedly into smaller tubes called bronchioles, forming a tree-like network. The bronchioles end in tiny air sacs called alveoli where gas exchange takes place.

passages.title: Alveoli and Gas Exchange
passages.text: Alveoli are tiny balloon-like air sacs at the end of the bronchioles and are the site of gas exchange. They have thin walls, a large surface area and a rich supply of blood capillaries. Oxygen diffuses from the alveoli into the blood while carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into the alveoli to be breathed out.

passages.title: Mechanism of Gas Exchange
passages.text: Gas exchange occurs by diffusion across the thin walls of the alveoli and capillaries. Oxygen moves from the high concentration in the alveoli into the blood, and carbon dioxide moves from the high concentration in the blood into the alveoli. The large surface area, thin walls, moist lining and rich blood supply make the alveoli highly efficient.

passages.title: The Diaphragm
passages.text: The diaphragm is a large dome-shaped sheet of muscle beneath the lungs that separates the chest from the abdomen. It plays a central role in breathing: when it contracts it flattens and increases the volume of the chest cavity, and when it relaxes it returns to a dome shape, decreasing the volume.

passages.title: Mechanism of Inhalation
passages.text: During inhalation the diaphragm contracts and flattens, and the external intercostal muscles contract to move the ribs up and out. This increases the volume of the chest cavity and lowers the pressure inside the lungs, so air rushes in from outside to equalise the pressure.

passages.title: Mechanism of Exhalation
passages.text: During exhalation the diaphragm relaxes and moves up, and the intercostal muscles relax so the ribs move down and in. This decreases the volume of the chest cavity and raises the pressure inside the lungs, forcing air out. Normal exhalation is largely a passive process.

passages.title: Oxygen Transport and Haemoglobin
passages.text: Oxygen is transported in the blood mainly by haemoglobin, a red pigment inside red blood cells. Haemoglobin binds oxygen in the lungs to form oxyhaemoglobin and releases it in the tissues where oxygen concentration is low. This allows the blood to carry far more oxygen than it could dissolve alone.

passages.title: Carbon Dioxide Transport
passages.text: Carbon dioxide produced by respiring cells is transported in the blood mostly as hydrogen carbonate ions dissolved in the plasma, with some carried by haemoglobin and some dissolved directly. It is released at the alveoli and breathed out during exhalation.

passages.title: The Larynx
passages.text: The larynx, or voice box, is located at the top of the trachea and contains the vocal cords. Air passing over the vocal cords makes them vibrate to produce sound. The epiglottis is a flap that covers the larynx during swallowing to prevent food entering the airway.

passages.title: Adaptations of Alveoli
passages.text: The alveoli are adapted for efficient gas exchange in several ways: they provide a very large total surface area, their walls are only one cell thick for a short diffusion distance, they have a moist lining so gases dissolve, and they are surrounded by many blood capillaries to maintain steep concentration gradients.

passages.title: Control of Breathing Rate
passages.text: Breathing rate is controlled by the brain, which monitors the level of carbon dioxide in the blood. During exercise, muscles produce more carbon dioxide, so breathing rate and depth increase to supply more oxygen and remove carbon dioxide faster. This keeps the blood gas levels balanced.

qa.question: What is the respiratory system?
qa.answer: The respiratory system is the group of organs that takes in oxygen and removes carbon dioxide, including the nose, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles and lungs.

qa.question: What is the difference between breathing and respiration?
qa.answer: Breathing is the physical movement of air in and out of the lungs, while respiration is the chemical release of energy from glucose inside cells.

qa.question: What is the function of the nasal cavity?
qa.answer: The nasal cavity warms, moistens and filters the incoming air, trapping dust and microbes with hairs and mucus.

qa.question: What is the function of the trachea?
qa.answer: The trachea carries air to the lungs; it is held open by C-shaped cartilage rings and lined with cilia and mucus that trap dust.

qa.question: What are alveoli and what is their function?
qa.answer: Alveoli are tiny air sacs at the end of the bronchioles where gas exchange occurs between the air and the blood.

qa.question: How does gas exchange occur in the lungs?
qa.answer: Gas exchange occurs by diffusion: oxygen diffuses from the alveoli into the blood, and carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into the alveoli.

qa.question: What happens during inhalation?
qa.answer: During inhalation the diaphragm contracts and flattens and the ribs move up and out, increasing chest volume and lowering pressure so air flows in.

qa.question: What happens during exhalation?
qa.answer: During exhalation the diaphragm relaxes and the ribs move down and in, decreasing chest volume and raising pressure so air is forced out.

qa.question: What is the role of the diaphragm in breathing?
qa.answer: The diaphragm is a dome-shaped muscle that contracts to increase chest volume during inhalation and relaxes to decrease it during exhalation.

qa.question: How is oxygen transported in the blood?
qa.answer: Oxygen is transported mainly by haemoglobin in red blood cells, forming oxyhaemoglobin, which releases oxygen in the tissues.

qa.question: How is carbon dioxide transported in the blood?
qa.answer: Carbon dioxide is transported mostly as hydrogen carbonate ions in the plasma, with some carried by haemoglobin and some dissolved.

qa.question: How are alveoli adapted for efficient gas exchange?
qa.answer: Alveoli have a large surface area, walls one cell thick, a moist lining and a rich blood supply, which maximise the rate of diffusion.

qa.question: What is the function of the larynx?
qa.answer: The larynx, or voice box, contains the vocal cords which vibrate as air passes over them to produce sound.

qa.question: What is the function of the epiglottis?
qa.answer: The epiglottis is a flap that covers the larynx during swallowing to stop food entering the trachea.

qa.question: How is breathing rate controlled?
qa.answer: The brain monitors carbon dioxide levels in the blood and increases breathing rate and depth when levels rise, such as during exercise.

qa.question: What are the bronchi and bronchioles?
qa.answer: The bronchi are the two tubes branching from the trachea into each lung, and bronchioles are the smaller branches that end in alveoli.

qa.question: True or False: Oxygen is transported mainly dissolved in blood plasma.
qa.answer: False. Oxygen is transported mainly by haemoglobin in red blood cells, not dissolved in plasma.

qa.question: Why does breathing rate increase during exercise?
qa.answer: During exercise muscles produce more carbon dioxide and need more oxygen, so breathing rate increases to supply oxygen and remove carbon dioxide.

qa.question: What is the pathway of air into the lungs?
qa.answer: Air passes through the nose, nasal cavity, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles and finally the alveoli.
